title: Review: Calorimetry; Measuring rates; Collision theory and factors
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: KN02#t2 term and clue written for the game; KN02#t4 term and clue written for the game; KN01#t1 term and clue written for the game; KN01#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN02#N.8, KN01#N.8a, KN02#N.4a, EN02#N.11a, KN01#N.3a, KN02#N.7a, EN02#N.13, KN02#N.2a, EN02#N.5a, KN02#N.9a. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Activation energy
items.clue: The minimum that an impact between particles must have for them to react, symbol Ea.

items.label: Surface area
items.clue: Increasing this for a solid exposes more particles, so collisions are more frequent.

items.label: Rate of reaction
items.clue: Change in the concentration of a substance per unit time, quoted as a positive value.

items.label: Tangent
items.clue: A straight line drawn at one time on the curve; its gradient gives the rate at that instant.

questions.stem: Why is the line after the highest reading extrapolated back to the time of mixing?

options.text: It removes random errors in the individual temperature readings.
It corrects for the heat absorbed by the cup and thermometer.
It shows the time at which the reaction finished and the temperature stopped rising.
It corrects for heat lost to the air while the reaction is still going.

questions.explanation: Heat escapes all the while the reaction runs. Extrapolating estimates the temperature reached if it had all happened at once, with no loss.

questions.stem: A student reacts 0.10 g of magnesium ribbon with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Which method is least suitable for measuring the rate of this reaction?

options.text: Collecting the hydrogen in a gas syringe and reading the volume every 10 s
Recording the loss in mass of the flask on a balance every 10 s
Taking samples at timed intervals, quenching them and titrating the acid left
Timing how long it takes to collect the first 20 cm³ of hydrogen in a gas syringe

questions.explanation: H₂ has a tiny molar mass: 0.10 g of Mg gives only about 0.008 g of H₂. A typical balance can barely detect the total loss, let alone the changes between readings.

questions.stem: Hydrogen iodide decomposes: 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g). A sample of hydrogen iodide is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What is the effect on the rate of reaction, and why?

options.text: It is unchanged: there are equal amounts of gas on both sides of the equation, so pressure has no effect.
It increases: the compressed molecules collide more energetically, so more collisions exceed Ea.
It increases: a larger amount of H₂ and I₂ can now form from the same amount of HI as before.
It increases: collisions become more frequent, and the fraction with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.

questions.stem: A spirit burner containing ethanol, C₂H₅OH, is used to heat 150.0 g of water in a copper can. Burning 0.920 g of ethanol raises the temperature of the water from 19.0 °C to 40.5 °C. Use c(water) = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ and Ar values H 1.01, C 12.01, O 16.00. What value of ΔH for the combustion of ethanol do these results give?

options.text: −6.75 × 10⁵ kJ mol⁻¹
−6.75 × 10² kJ mol⁻¹
−9.25 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹
−1.35 × 10¹ kJ mol⁻¹

questions.stem: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Which quantity is the rate of this reaction at a particular moment?

options.text: The total time taken for all of the H₂O₂ in the sample to decompose
The total volume of O₂ given off by the time the reaction has stopped
The decrease in the concentration of H₂O₂ per unit time at that moment
The concentration of H₂O₂ at that moment divided by the time elapsed so far

questions.explanation: Rate is the change in concentration per unit time, in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. At a moment, it is the gradient of the tangent, quoted as positive.

questions.stem: Which statement explains how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction at constant temperature?

options.text: It gives the reacting particles more kinetic energy, so more collisions exceed Ea.
It increases the concentration of the reactants, so collisions happen more often.
It makes the reaction more exothermic, so more energy is available for collisions.
It provides a route with a lower Ea, so a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy.

questions.explanation: Same particles, same energies, but a lower barrier. More collisions now have E ≥ Ea, so more succeed each second.

questions.stem: A student measures the enthalpy change when potassium chloride dissolves in water. The temperature falls. The student uses a thin glass beaker with no lid instead of an insulated cup. How does the student's value of ΔH compare with the accepted value?

options.text: Less positive: energy flows in from the warmer room, so the fall in temperature is too small.
More positive: heat escapes from the solution to the room, so the fall in temperature is too big.
Less positive: the glass gives out cold to the room, so the fall in temperature is too small.
The same: ΔH depends only on the amount of KCl dissolved, not on the container.

questions.stem: In a mixture of two gases at room temperature, each molecule collides with others billions of times every second, yet the reaction between them is slow. Why do most of these collisions not lead to a reaction?

options.text: Most collisions have less energy than ΔH, the energy that the reaction gives out.
Most collisions have less energy than Ea, the minimum needed for a reaction.
A catalyst must be present in each collision before any bonds can break.
Most of the molecules are moving far too slowly to collide with one another.

questions.explanation: Only collisions with energy of at least Ea lead to reaction. At room temperature that is a tiny fraction, so the reaction is slow.

questions.stem: 50.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is placed in a polystyrene cup and 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is added. The temperature of the mixture rises by 4.50 °C. HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l). Assume that the solutions have a density of 1.00 g cm⁻³ and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.text: −28.2 kJ mol⁻¹
−37.6 kJ mol⁻¹
−1.41 kJ mol⁻¹
−56.4 kJ mol⁻¹

questions.stem: An iron nail held in a Bunsen flame only glows. The same mass of fine iron filings sprinkled into the flame burns in bright sparks. Why do the filings react so much faster with oxygen?

options.text: The filings are hotter than the nail, so their collisions with oxygen are more energetic.
Iron in small pieces has a lower activation energy for its reaction with oxygen.
The filings expose a far larger surface area, so collisions with oxygen are far more frequent.
The filings contain more iron atoms in total, so they release more energy.

questions.explanation: In a nail, most iron atoms are buried inside. In filings, far more atoms are on a surface, so many more successful collisions happen each second.
